beats.lead: You have probably heard this rule
beats.text: You cannot fold paper more than seven or eight times.
beats.note: True for an ordinary sheet. It was never a law of mathematics, only a limit nobody had bothered to break.

beats.name: Britney Gallivan
beats.role: A California high-school student solving a fold-count challenge for extra credit. She proved it first on a folded strip of gold, then set out to do it with paper.

beats.text: She folded a single sheet twelve times.
beats.note: The sheet was a strip of tissue paper about 1,219 metres long, three quarters of a mile, because length is what a fold count actually costs.

beats.context: How much more paper the twelfth fold consumes than the first, by Gallivan's own equation. Not a guess; exponential growth, counted.

beats.text: She did not break the rule. She worked out why it existed.

beats.line: The limit was never eight folds. It was arithmetic.
